questions.stem: What volume is occupied by 0.5 mol of nitrogen gas at s.t.p.? [molar volume at s.t.p. = 22.4 dm3/mol]
questions.explanation: Volume = number of moles x molar volume = 0.5 x 22.4 = 11.2 dm3. Because Avogadro's law makes the molar volume the same for every gas, the identity of the gas does not enter the calculation at all.

distractorRationale.a: 0.25 mol was used instead of 0.5 mol
distractorRationale.c: The molar volume was quoted without applying the 0.5 factor
distractorRationale.d: The molar volume was multiplied by 2 instead of by 0.5

questions.stem: What is the mass of 2.24 dm3 of sulphur(IV) oxide, SO2, measured at s.t.p.? [S = 32, O = 16; molar volume = 22.4 dm3/mol]
questions.explanation: Moles of gas = 2.24 / 22.4 = 0.1 mol. The molar mass of SO2 is 32 + (2 x 16) = 64 g/mol, so the mass is 0.1 x 64 = 6.4 g.

distractorRationale.a: A molar mass of 32 was used, as if the gas were oxygen rather than sulphur(IV) oxide
distractorRationale.c: The relative atomic mass of sulphur alone was quoted
distractorRationale.d: The molar mass was given as the answer, ignoring the 0.1 mol factor

questions.stem: 40 cm3 of carbon monoxide is burned in oxygen according to 2CO(g) + O2(g) -> 2CO2(g). What volume of oxygen is required, all volumes being measured at the same temperature and pressure?
questions.explanation: By Avogadro's law the volume ratio for gases equals the mole ratio, so CO : O2 is 2 : 1. Half as much oxygen as carbon monoxide is needed, giving 40 / 2 = 20 cm3. The reaction would also produce 40 cm3 of carbon dioxide.

distractorRationale.a: The ratio was applied twice, dividing 40 by 4
distractorRationale.c: The ratio was treated as 1 : 1, ignoring the coefficient 2 on CO
distractorRationale.d: The ratio was inverted, doubling instead of halving

questions.stem: Avogadro's law states that equal volumes of all gases under the same conditions of temperature and pressure contain the same number of
questions.explanation: Avogadro's law is stated in terms of molecules. It holds because the molecules of a gas are so far apart that their own size and mutual attractions are negligible, so what determines the volume is simply how many particles are present, not what they are.

distractorRationale.a: Atom counts differ because gases may be monatomic, diatomic or polyatomic
distractorRationale.c: Proton numbers vary widely between different gases
distractorRationale.d: Equal volumes of different gases have very different masses, as hydrogen and carbon dioxide show

questions.stem: Calculate the volume in dm3 occupied by 8 g of oxygen gas at s.t.p. [O = 16; molar volume = 22.4 dm3/mol]
questions.explanation: Oxygen gas is diatomic, so its molar mass is 32 g/mol. Moles = 8 / 32 = 0.25 mol, and volume = 0.25 x 22.4 = 5.6 dm3. Using 16 instead of 32 as the molar mass is the usual error and would double the answer.

questions.stem: A gas has a vapour density of 22. Its relative molecular mass is
questions.explanation: Vapour density compares the mass of a volume of gas with the mass of the same volume of hydrogen, and hydrogen is diatomic with a relative molecular mass of 2. Therefore relative molecular mass = 2 x vapour density = 2 x 22 = 44, which corresponds to carbon dioxide.

distractorRationale.a: The vapour density was halved instead of doubled
distractorRationale.b: Vapour density and relative molecular mass were treated as the same quantity
distractorRationale.d: The vapour density was multiplied by 4, as if hydrogen had a relative molecular mass of 4
